output:
You buy insurance so that someone else pays when things go wrong. But the insurer does not pay from the very first penny. A deductible is the slice of each claim you cover yourself before their money starts flowing.

Say your car policy carries a £500 deductible and a storm causes £3,000 of damage. You pay the first £500. The insurer pays the remaining £2,500. If a falling branch only dents your bumper and the repair costs £400, you pay all of it and the insurer pays nothing at all.

Think of it as the gap at the bottom of a door. Small things blow under it and never reach you. Only larger trouble is big enough to be stopped and dealt with.

Insurers do this for two reasons. It spares them the cost of processing thousands of tiny claims. It also makes you a little more careful, because you have skin in the game.

Here is the trade-off that matters when choosing a policy. A higher deductible means cheaper monthly premiums but a bigger bill when disaster strikes. A lower deductible costs more every month and less on the day you need it.

In short, a deductible is the agreed amount you absorb yourself, with the insurer catching whatever sits above it.
